name.display: Enslaved persons in the United States and its colonial predecessors

count.basis: Persons enslaved in the United States at the 1860 census. Not a figure for the whole period.

persons.harm: Enslavement and its constituent offenses; see CL-CHATTEL-ENSLAVEMENT
persons.attestation: Existence attested in aggregate by census, probate, bill of sale, ship manifest, plantation ledger, and Freedmen's Bureau record. The individuating sources - narrative, petition, register - reach a small fraction of those recorded.
persons.note: This row is a count and is marked as one. It does not stand for individuals and must not be read as a person. Named individuals appear below where a source preserved a name. The disproportion between this number and that list is the principal finding of this register.

persons.place: Talbot County, Maryland; later Massachusetts, New York, and Washington, D.C.
persons.role: Narrator; formerly enslaved; abolitionist, editor, and United States Marshal for the District of Columbia
persons.harm: Enslavement from birth; separation from his mother in infancy; whipping and hiring out; denial of literacy by law

voice.words: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
voice.citation: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845), ch. X

persons.consent_note: Recorded because the injury is recorded. No claim is asserted on this person's behalf by this book. See METHODOLOGY.md section 7.

persons.role: Narrator; formerly enslaved; writing as Linda Brent
persons.harm: Enslavement; sustained sexual coercion by her enslaver, an offense not cognizable at law because she was property; seven years concealed in a crawlspace to escape him

voice.words: Slavery is terrible for men; but it is far more terrible for women.
voice.citation: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861), ch. XIV

persons.note: Her narrative records a category of crime for which no forum has ever existed in any entry of this book: sexual violence against an enslaved woman was not an offense in any slaveholding state, because the law recognized no injury to property from its owner.
persons.consent_note: Recorded because the injury is recorded. No claim is asserted on this person's behalf by this book. See METHODOLOGY.md section 7.

persons.role: Narrator; formerly enslaved; litigant
persons.harm: Enslavement; her son Peter was sold illegally out of New York to Alabama in violation of the state's emancipation statute

voice.citation: The widely reproduced 'Ar'n't I a Woman' text of the 1851 Akron speech is Frances Dana Gage's 1863 reconstruction. Marius Robinson's contemporaneous 1851 report differs materially and contains no such refrain.

persons.note: Standing is recorded as claimant because she sued in 1828 to recover Peter and won, one of the earliest instances of a Black woman prevailing against a white man in an American court. The voice field is left contested rather than filled with the familiar text: the book does not print a reconstruction as a quotation. That the most quoted words attributed to her are probably not hers is itself a record of how testimony survives.

persons.place: Brooks County, Georgia; killed near Barney, Lowndes County
persons.role: Farm worker; wife of Hayes Turner
persons.harm: Seized and killed by a mob the day after publicly denouncing her husband's lynching and stating she would swear out warrants against those responsible. She was eight months pregnant; the child was killed also.
persons.note: She was twenty-one or thereabouts. The precise manner of the killing is documented in Walter White's NAACP investigation and is not reproduced here; the citation is sufficient and the detail is not owed to the reader.
persons.consent_note: Recorded because the injury is recorded. No claim is asserted on this person's behalf by this book. See METHODOLOGY.md section 7.

persons.harm: Taken from custody and lynched. His body was left hanging for two days.

name.display: Name unrecorded - the unborn child of Mary Turner

persons.harm: Killed in the course of their mother's killing
persons.attestation: Existence attested by every account of the event, including the NAACP field investigation. No name was given and none could have been. The child was at or near term.
persons.note: This row exists to demonstrate the rule in METHODOLOGY.md section 7. A distinct person, attested by the sources, without a name, gets a row. Folding this death into the count for Brooks and Lowndes would record it a second time as a loss. No pronoun is recorded for this child, and none is supplied.

name.display: Residents and property owners of the Greenwood District

count.basis: 39 deaths confirmed by the 2001 Oklahoma Commission, which reviewed estimates up to 300. More than 1,250 homes destroyed; approximately 6,000 people detained.

persons.harm: Killed; detained; dispossessed of homes, businesses, churches, a hospital, schools, and land
persons.attestation: Searches for mass graves under the direction of the City of Tulsa have recovered remains that are being examined and, where possible, identified by DNA. Identification work is ongoing.
persons.note: This is the one entry in the register where the count may still decrease in favour of names. The identification project is the only active effort in this book to convert a number back into people.

name.display: Men enrolled in the United States Public Health Service study at Tuskegee, and their families

count.basis: 399 men with latent syphilis and 201 controls. Wives infected and children born with congenital syphilis were never fully enumerated.

persons.harm: Deceived as to their diagnosis; denied treatment that existed; observed to autopsy
persons.attestation: Individually named in the study's own records, which the Public Health Service maintained meticulously for forty years. The identities exist because the perpetrators kept them.
persons.note: This register entry is recorded as collective for privacy, not for want of names. The men are individually identified in the surviving federal records. The last surviving participant died in 2004.

name.display: Persons recorded as lynched in the United States, 1889-1918

count.basis: NAACP compilation, 1919. 702 of those recorded were white. The compilers state that the count is incomplete because it depends on press reporting.

persons.place: The United States, concentrated in the former Confederate states
persons.harm: Killed by mobs outside any legal process
persons.attestation: The NAACP compilation names a substantial portion of the dead, by date, place, and alleged cause. Where it does not, no source does.
persons.note: This row is the register's largest count and its plainest statement of what the register cannot do. Each of these 3,224 is entitled under this book's own rule to an individuated row. Producing them requires archival work in the sources listed, county by county, and is the standing task this repository exists to hold.
persons.consent_note: Recorded because the injury is recorded. No claim is asserted on this person's behalf by this book. See METHODOLOGY.md section 7.
